title: Spindrift: Learning quantum degeneracy from thermal purity in restricted path integral Monte Carlo
abstract: Restricted path integral Monte Carlo (RPIMC) sidesteps the fluctuating Fermion sign problem by confining paths within nodal pockets of a trial density matrix, thereby recovering polynomial scaling. However, this nodal surface must be provided from elsewhere; unless it is exact, it introduces a fixed-node energy error.   Here we introduce \textsc{Spindrift}, a Variational Density Matrix approach that learns the many-body Fermionic density matrix from a regularised Bloch residual, evaluated on samples drawn by a restricted Worm algorithm. Motivated by the observation of the `purity' of quantum mechanics at high temperature (where kinetic energy dominates), we train the density matrix along a temperature (imaginary time) curriculum, learning increasingly large \emph{corrections} to the initial free-particle reference. We parametrise our model with a permutation-equivariant continuous normalising flow to generate quasi-particle backflow trajectories, modulated by a symmetric Jastrow factor. This architecture guarantees exact Fermionic antisymmetry and spatial symmetry throughout training.   Simulating $N=3$ interacting Fermions in a two-dimensional harmonic trap, we demonstrate stable curriculum training. The learnt velocity field smoothly deforms the nodal structure away from the free-particle reference. Open-Worm G-sector trapping provides a natural diagnostic for nodal accuracy.   Although the current lack of a nodal action in our estimator precludes absolute benchmarking, \textsc{Spindrift} lowers the restricted thermodynamic energy relative to the free-particle reference at each temperature, establishing a stable, physics-informed framework for finite-temperature quantum Monte Carlo where the nodal structure is learnt self-consistently.
summary: Spindrift introduces a novel Variational Density Matrix approach that uses continuous normalising flows to learn the complex nodal structure of the thermal density matrix in restricted Path Integral Monte Carlo simulations. By training this model across an imaginary time curriculum, it bypasses the need for pre-supplied node information, establishing a self-consistent framework for studying interacting fermions at finite temperatures.
main_problem: The primary challenge is overcoming the Fermion sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo simulations, which limits the accurate calculation of ground state and finite-temperature properties.
main_result: The proposed method, Spindrift, successfully trains a variational density matrix that self-consistently learns the nodal structure across an imaginary time curriculum, yielding lower energy estimates than free-particle references.
method: It employs a Variational Density Matrix approach parameterized by a permutation-equivariant continuous normalising flow (CNF) to generate quasi-particle backflow trajectories. Training is performed via curriculum learning using the Bloch residual as the loss function.
model_or_system: The study focuses on $N=3$ interacting spin-polarized Fermions confined in a two-dimensional harmonic trap. The simulation evolves the thermal density matrix ($ho$) from high temperature towards quantum degeneracy.
key_observables: Mixed energy estimator, Bloch residual ($E_{	ext{res}}$), and mean backflow displacement magnitude are tracked as diagnostics for nodal accuracy and convergence.
important_parameters: The imaginary time/temperature curriculum ($ eta$ progression) is crucial, moving from high temperature ($ eta 	o 0$) to quantum degeneracy ($ eta=1$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the density matrix can be accurately parameterized by a CNF augmented with a Jastrow factor. A key limitation is the lack of an explicit nodal action in the estimator.
figures_summary: Figures track energy estimators, Bloch residuals, and backflow displacement across temperature stages ($ eta=0.2$ to $1.0$), demonstrating the smooth deformation of the nodal structure as quantum correlations build up.
paper_structure: The paper introduces Spindrift as a solution to the sign problem in PIMC by learning $ho$. It details the CNF architecture and training strategy using curriculum learning on the Bloch residual, culminating in energy comparisons against known limits.
why_interesting: This work represents a significant advancement in applying deep generative models (CNFs) to solve fundamental many-body quantum simulation problems, providing a self-consistent way to handle nodal structure which is central to fermionic physics.
